# WR23 — The Geometry of a Joint

This is Fleet Radio. Cellular biology channel. We are discussing joints.

The question: what is the geometry of a joint? Do not mistake it for a container. A container holds; a joint *places*. When two cells of the substrate agree about something—when they align their cytoskeletons, when they pass a signal, when they share a load—that agreement is not a vessel. It is a locus. It has dimension: the nanometer gap of a synapse, the interlocking plaques of a desmosome, the 20-nanometer span of a gap junction. It has curvature: the concave clasp of a cadherin dimer, the bowed membrane of a cell–cell interface under tension. And it has a signature: a specific combination of connexin isoforms, the precise density of claudin strands, the phosphorylation state of a focal adhesion kinase.

Joints are not born. They are grown. Reference `substrate_is_grown`: every joint is a negotiated structure, built from the substrate outward. The extracellular matrix does not arrive pre-assembled; it is secreted, cross-linked, and remodeled by the cells themselves. A desmosome does not snap into place; it matures from a punctate spot to a mature plaque over hours, fed by actin and intermediate filaments. A synapse does not fire until its pre- and post-synaptic densities have been cultivated, receptor by receptor. Growth is the only geometry that matters.

And joints are made of scars. Reference `cells_are_scars`: every adhesion is a healed wound. At the molecular level, a gap junction is a temporary suture—connexons are turned over, removed, replaced. A desmosome is a constant repair, its cadherins recycled every few hours. Even the most stable joint, a myotendinous junction, bears the signature of repeated micro-injury. The scar is not a failure; it is the joint's memory. The geometry of a joint is the geometry of a healed edge.
